edits.new: The 18 betaine-reducer models excreted 48–192 mmol of TMA per gram of biomass formed; at the assumed 0.06 methane per TMA (Methods), their measured biomass would supply the measured emissions at doubling times of 1.0 h to 35 h, and their methane per unit of growth was not correlated with the emissions either (Spearman ρ = −0.26, n = 6; Figure 7).

edits.old: requiring substantially more adjustments in the slope and th
edits.new: Methane from betaine depends on a second organism that converts the TMA, and only one species among the MAGs carries *mcrA*: *Methanolobus*.1, whose curated model released 126 mmol of methane per gram of biomass formed on methylamines (120–159 mmol g⁻¹ across published ion couplings), about 2,900 times the MPn consumers’ yield at a ratio of 0.07. Because a methanogen also spends methane on maintenance, its required specific methanogenic activity is the more direct measure: given its measured biomass, the measured emissions require 2–21 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ in the R1 cores and 60–99 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ in the R2 cores, equivalent to growth-coupled doubling times of 4.2 h to 38 h and 53 min to 1.5 h. Methanogens not recovered as MAGs lower these requirements but do not remove them. In all sequenced reads of the six cores, *mcrA* was 1.7 times as abundant as the *Methanolobus* MAG (several-fold only in three R2 samples where the MAG was scarce and *mcrA* reads few, 16–66 per sample), and 42% of the *mcrA* reads came from other methanogens, mostly *Methanohalophilus*, *Methanogenium* and *Methanococcoides*, 93% of them in no assembled contig. With the methanogens’ biomass scaled to the *mcrA* reads, the measured emissions require 1–9 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ in the R1 cores and 19–44 mmol g⁻¹ h⁻¹ in the R2 cores (doubling times of 9.4 h to 3 d and 2.0 h to 4.7 h). Doubling every few hours, as in the R2 cores, still seems unlikely for sediment methanogens unless non-growth methanogenesis or a lower DNA content of biomass add to the methane. The standing porewater pools of mono-, di- and trimethylamine could supply the measured emissions if turned over every 0.9–3.4 days, and supplying the TMA for complete conversion would need the betaine reducers to double only every 37 h to 54 d. Neither the methanogens’ biomass (Spearman ρ = −0.43 for the MAG and −0.66 counting all *mcrA* reads, p ≥ 0.17) nor that of any other guild followed the differences in emissions among the six cores.
edits.rationale: betaine -> TMA -> methanogen chain; required specific activity first; R1/R2 contrast; methanogens in the reads

edits.new: In the models, each methylphosphonate consumed yields exactly one methane (1 methane : 1 methylphosphonate), whereas methane from betaine was set by assumption to 0.06 of the TMA excreted (Methods).
edits.rationale: CH4/MePn is 1.000 for every MAG and core in saltern_fluxes.json at 0.07 and 0.33, in every committed version (c49e503, a725dce, 1b758a4) and in the substrate-addition run. The 1.4 is not supported. Betaine CH4 = 0.06 × TMA is the Methods assumption (P36), not a model result.

edits.old: This was mechanistically corroborated by metabolic models that reproduced the experimental methane emissions with high accuracy (R2 = 0.978), and demonstrate that methane is generated stoichiometrically from methylphosphonate.
edits.new: Metabolic models show why: a C–P lyase releases one methane per methylphosphonate cleaved for phosphorus, so the modeled MPn consumers released only 0.04–0.66 mmol of methane per gram of biomass formed, about 2,900 times less than the methylotrophic methanogen, for which methane is the product of its energy metabolism. Their measured biomass could supply the measured emissions only at doubling times of minutes to hours, whereas the methanogens’ would need doubling times of hours to days in the R1 cores and one to five hours in the R2 cores, also when the methanogens found only in the reads are counted; neither guild’s biomass followed the differences in emissions among the six cores.

edits.old: Metabolic models were developed using dereplicated medium and high quality
edits.new: Metabolic models were built for the representative MAG of each MPn-consumer and betaine-reducer species of the re-assembled MAG set (39 and 18 species; Table 4), one model per species and guild. Prodigal genes were annotated with the RAST service (53), and draft models were built with ModelSEEDpy, which implements the KBase modeling pipeline (52), from the current ModelSEED templates with our curations (Gram-negative v7, Gram-positive v7 and Archaea v6 templates for 31, 19 and 6 models, respectively). RAST alone was chosen over drafts that also used KOfam, eggNOG-mapper v2.1.13 and Bakta v1.12.0 annotations by criteria fixed in advance (gene-associated and gapfilled reactions, guild-pathway support, ATP production without a carbon source, and the fraction of blocked reactions): the added annotations raised the number of gene-associated reactions, but they also raised the fraction of blocked reactions by 2.7–6.5 percentage points, beyond the pre-set limit of 2, and the two that included eggNOG-mapper let one model make ATP from ammonia and oxygen. ATP production was corrected on 54 test media, and the models were gapfilled as in the original protocol: MPn consumers first on aerobic lactate with phosphate and then on lactate with MPn as the only phosphorus source, after a C–P lyase pathway and an MPn transporter were added where absent; betaine reducers on aerobic lactate, after which betaine reductase, glycine reductase and TMA export were added. Reactions that let a model oxidize ammonia (reversed nitrite and hydroxylamine reductases) or consume methane without annotation support were restricted to their reductive or methane-producing directions, and models that lost growth were gapfilled again. One MPn-consumer model (JASFMS01.1) could not grow and was excluded, leaving 38 MPn-consumer and 18 betaine-reducer models; none of the MPn-consumer models required MPn to grow. The model of the only *mcrA*-carrying species among the MAGs (*Methanolobus*.1) grew by converting methyl groups to acetate instead of methane, because it could not reduce methanophenazine; its F420H2 dehydrogenase (Fpo), membrane-bound heterodisulfide reductase (HdrDE), Rnf complex and methyl-coenzyme M reductase were corrected to the gene-supported forms, after which it grew by methylotrophic methanogenesis on mono-, di- and trimethylamine, with the textbook methane yields, but not on methanol (its genome lacks *mtaB* and *mtaC*). A gene annotated by RAST as methane monooxygenase in two *Roseovarius* models is a propane 2-monooxygenase (*prmA*), and its reaction was disabled.
edits.rationale: curated methanogen (models/methanogen/CURATION.md) and PrmA block (pipeline/apply_prma_block.py)

edits.old: for direct comparison and consistent flux interpretation
edits.new: The biomass of each member in each core was its relative abundance times the soil DNA concentration of each depth, summed over the two layers (0–5 and 5–15 cm) with a soil bulk density of 0.7 g cm⁻³ estimated from other studies of this region, and with DNA taken as 10% of dry biomass. The product of a guild’s methane yield and its biomass is the methane it produces per unit of growth; dividing the measured emission by this product gives the specific growth rate µ at which the guild’s measured biomass would supply the measured emission (doubling time ln 2 / µ), and, for the methanogen, dividing by its biomass alone gives the specific methanogenic activity required. If DNA were 3% of dry biomass, every biomass would be 3.3 times larger and every required rate 3.3 times smaller. Spearman rank correlations (exact permutation p values) between each guild’s methane per unit of growth and the measured emissions of the six unrestored cores test whether the models follow the differences among cores. To include guild members not recovered as MAGs, each guild’s biomass was also scaled, in each sample, by the copies of its marker gene per genome equivalent in all sequenced reads (*mcrA* for methanogens, *phnJ* for MPn consumers, *grdI* for betaine reducers; see Metagenomics) divided by its MAGs’ genomes per genome equivalent. The required specific methanogenic activity does not depend on the methane yield; the doubling times computed from the read-based methanogen biomass assume that every *mcrA*-carrying organism has the yield of the *Methanolobus* model.
edits.rationale: explicit-rate comparison; the 10 % DNA constant and its sensitivity are stated; read-based scaling

edits.old: reveals that generally the models predict half
edits.new: At a ratio of 0.33 (at least 0.33 mol of methylphosphonate per mol of inorganic phosphate, about 25% of the phosphate taken up) the yield rose to 0.164 mmol g⁻¹, and the required doubling times to 8 min to 56 min; even with methylphosphonate as the only phosphorus source the yield reached only 0.66 mmol g⁻¹, and the doubling times 31 min to 3.8 h. C–P lyase (*phnJ*) genes were 1.7–2.4 times as abundant in all sequenced reads as in the MPn-consumer MAGs, so counting MPn consumers not recovered as MAGs lengthens these doubling times only to 4 min to 28 min at a ratio of 0.07 and 1.1 h to 7.1 h with methylphosphonate as the only phosphorus source (Figure 7b, open symbols). Such rates are implausibly fast for sediment microorganisms, so assimilation of methylphosphonate by the modeled consumers cannot supply the measured emissions unless methylphosphonate is degraded well beyond the phosphorus they assimilate (for example, with the phosphate excreted or stored as polyphosphate), which the models do not represent.

edits.new: To compare the hypothesized methane sources (Figure 10), the abundance of each pathway was taken from its marker gene in all reads and from its MAGs (see Metagenomics); the *mcrA* reads were assigned to methylotrophic, hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic methanogens by the genus of their best hit, pooled over the 12 samples of the unrestored cores (reads of the ANME-1-related Methanophagales were excluded), and only the archaeal reads of the methanol methyltransferase gene (*mtaB*) were counted. The standing porewater pool of each measured substrate was its NMR concentration times the porewater volume of each layer (porosity 0.74, from the bulk density of 0.7 g cm⁻³ and a particle density of 2.65 g cm⁻³), converted to methane with the stoichiometry of methanogenesis (methane per molecule: TMA 2.25, DMA 1.5, MMA 0.75, methanol 0.75, formate 0.25, acetate 1, and glycine betaine 2.25 through TMA); the pool divided by the measured emission is the turnover time at which it would supply the emission. To apportion the emission among the pathways, each guild’s methane per unit of growth (yield × read-based biomass) was compared at equal specific growth rates, and the methanogens’ share was divided among the methanogen groups by their *mcrA* reads.
edits.rationale: Methods for Figure 10 and the attribution

edits.new: Figure 10 sets the hypothesized methane sources side by side. Among the pathway genes in all reads, C–P lyase (*phnJ*) was the most abundant (9–18 copies per 100 genome equivalents; 5–9 genomes per 100 in the MAGs), mostly of *Roseovarius* and *Marivita*, followed by the TMA-producing betaine reductase (*grdI*; 1–12; mostly M55B127, UBA8670 and DATFJG01) and choline and carnitine genes (*cutC* + *cntA*; 2–10), whereas methanogens were rare (*mcrA* 0.1–0.8). Of the *mcrA* reads, 91% belonged to methylotrophic methanogens (*Methanolobus*, *Methanohalophilus*, *Methanococcoides*, and hydrogen-dependent Methanomassiliicoccales), 9% to hydrogenotrophic methanogens, mostly *Methanogenium*, and 3 reads to the acetoclastic *Methanothrix* and *Methanocrinis*. Only 21% of the reads of the methanol methyltransferase gene *mtaB* were archaeal (mostly *Methanohalophilus* and *Methanococcoides*), and no MAG carried methanol-, hydrogen- or acetate-based methanogenesis. The measured porewater pools would supply the measured emissions if turned over every 0.9–3.4 days (mono-, di- and trimethylamine), 0.6–3.0 days (methanol), 4–12 hours (formate), 8–335 days (acetate) and 61–168 days (glycine betaine, if fully converted through TMA). The betaine reducers could supply the TMA for complete conversion at doubling times of 37 hours or longer, whereas the acetoclastic methanogens, at their read-based abundance, would need doubling times of minutes.
edits.rationale: Results for Figure 10

edits.old: although methylphosphonate degradation by halophilic aerobic bacteria such as Halomonas appears to be the most corroborated conclusion from multiple perspectives.
edits.new: and methylphosphonate degradation by halophilic aerobic bacteria. Combining the read, MAG, substrate and model evidence attributes most of the methane to methylotrophic methanogenesis, with methylphosphonate degradation a secondary source (Figure 10).
edits.rationale: Conclusions opening agrees with the synthesis

edits.new: Taken together, these results attribute most of the measured methane to methylotrophic methanogenesis (Figure 10). Methanogens that use methyl groups carry 91% of the methanogen *mcrA* reads, hydrogenotrophic methanogens 9%, and acetoclastic methanogens fewer than 1%, although acetate was abundant. Their substrates are mainly methylated amines (the dominant *Methanolobus* cannot use methanol, which only the less abundant *Methanohalophilus* and *Methanococcoides* may use): the porewater mono-, di- and trimethylamine would supply the measured emissions if turned over every 0.9–3.4 days, and the large glycine betaine pool (enough for 61–168 days of emissions if fully converted through TMA), degraded by abundant betaine-reducing Bacillota, together with choline and carnitine degradation, can resupply TMA without fast growth. Methylphosphonate degradation by C–P lyase bacteria (mostly *Roseovarius* and *Marivita* in situ, and *Halomonas* in culture) does contribute, but it is limited by their phosphorus demand: at equal specific growth rates the MPn consumers would supply 1–7% of the methane at an MPn:Pi uptake ratio of 0.07, 3–24% at 0.33, and 9–55% only if methylphosphonate were their sole phosphorus source; even growing ten times faster than the methanogens, they would supply 6–45% at a ratio of 0.07. Growth-coupled production does not close the budget of the R2 cores: at a doubling time of one day, the methanogens there would supply only 8–19% of the measured methane, so their methane must come largely from activity beyond growth (19–45 mmol CH₄ per gram of methanogen biomass per hour) or from more methanogen biomass than the DNA suggests. In the microcosms, only the TMA addition produced as much methane as the controls under anoxic conditions (Figure 4b), and methylphosphonic acid did not raise methane significantly above the controls under oxic conditions (Figure 4a). We therefore attribute the measured methane mainly to methylotrophic methanogenesis fed by the turnover of compatible solutes, with methylphosphonate degradation as a secondary, phosphorus-limited source and hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis as a minor one.
edits.rationale: the synthesis paragraph the user asked for (attribution among the hypotheses)

edits.old: We therefore propose methylphosphonate as the primary source of methane in the hypersaline unrestored salterns. The C-P lyase pathway in aerobic halotolerant bacteria appears to be the precise mechanism.
edits.new: We therefore propose that the methane of the hypersaline unrestored salterns comes mainly from methylotrophic methanogens that use methylated amines derived from compatible solutes, and secondarily from the C–P lyase pathway of aerobic halotolerant bacteria degrading methylphosphonate.
edits.rationale: the proposal agrees with the synthesis paragraph (replaces the P100 'Consider revising' comment)

The attribution rests on the read survey (all 2.08 billion reads), the MAGs, the porewater pools and the per-gram models; the shares assume equal specific growth rates of the guilds, with sensitivities given in the text. If the authors prefer to keep methylphosphonate as the primary source, the Abstract, the Introduction (P24) and the models section would need evidence that methylphosphonate is degraded far beyond assimilatory phosphorus demand.

figure10.caption: Figure 10. The hypothesized methane sources of the unrestored salterns. (a) Pathways: cleavage of methylphosphonate (MPn) by C–P lyase (blue); degradation of glycine betaine, choline and carnitine to TMA (orange), which feeds methylotrophic methanogenesis (dashed); and methanogenesis from methylamines, methanol, H₂/CO₂ or formate, and acetate (green). (b) Abundance per 100 genome equivalents in all reads (open: copies of *phnJ*, *grdI*, *cutC* + *cntA*, *mcrA* split by the methanogen group of the reads’ best hits, and the archaeal share of *mtaB*) and in the MAGs (filled: genomes of the guild’s species), median and range over the 12 samples of the six unrestored cores. (c) The most abundant organisms: genus of the reads’ best hits (share of the pathway’s reads) and the most abundant MAG species. (d) Turnover each pathway alone would need to supply the measured methane of the six cores: turnover of the measured porewater pool (diamonds; methane per molecule: TMA 2.25, DMA 1.5, MMA 0.75, methanol 0.75, formate 0.25, acetate 1, glycine betaine 2.25 through TMA), and doubling time of the pathway’s organisms (squares; per-gram yields × measured biomass as in Figure 7, MAG-based filled, read-based open; MPn consumers at an MPn:Pi uptake ratio of 0.07 and with MPn as the only phosphorus source; betaine reducers supplying TMA for complete conversion). Hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic methanogens have no model; their doubling times at the methylotrophic model’s yield are lower bounds (dotted; a lower growth yield allows slower growth). Methylphosphonic acid was detected but not quantified; choline, carnitine and H₂ were not measured.
